ai.literal: Board without, game-piece having played, like that indeed: complete book without, assembly taking part.
ai.translation: Taking part in an assembly without complete learning is exactly like playing a game with pieces but no board.
ai.modern: முழுமையான நூலறிவு இல்லாமல் கற்றவர் அவையில் சென்று பேசுவது, கட்டம் வரைந்த பலகை இல்லாமல் வட்டு விளையாடுவதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid analogy to show the futility of an uneducated person trying to participate in a learned discussion. It compares such an attempt to playing a board game ('வட்டு') without the board ('அரங்கு') that defines the rules and spaces. Just as the game pieces have no meaning without the board, a person's words have no weight in an assembly ('கோட்டி') without the solid foundation of complete learning ('நிரம்பிய நூல்'). The emphatic 'ஏ' in 'அற்றே' stresses that the two situations are exactly alike.

ai.literal: Unlearned man speech desiring, breasts both lacking woman womanhood having desired like that.
ai.translation: An unlearned man desiring to speak is like a woman lacking both breasts desiring womanhood.
ai.modern: கல்வி கற்காதவன் அவையில் பேச விரும்புவது, இரண்டு மார்பகங்களும் இல்லாத ஒருத்தி பெண்மையை விரும்பியதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a striking physical analogy to illustrate the futility of an unlearned person trying to participate in scholarly discourse. The phrase 'கல்லாதான் சொல் காமுறுதல்' describes an uneducated man's desire to speak or give an address. The poet compares this to a woman lacking both breasts ('முலை இரண்டும் இல்லாதாள்') who still desires to experience or display womanhood ('பெண் காமுற்று'). Just as the physical attribute is considered essential for the latter in this imagery, learning is the indispensable foundation for speaking with authority.

ai.literal: Even the unlearned are very good, learned people in front of, without speaking to remain if they manage.
ai.translation: Even the unlearned are considered very good, if they can manage to remain silent in the presence of the learned.
ai.modern: கற்றவர்களுக்கு முன்னால் எதுவும் பேசாமல் அமைதியாக இருக்க முடிந்தால், கல்லாதவர்களும் மிகவும் நல்லவர்களே ஆவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the value of silence for those who lack education. The phrase kallatavarum nani nallar states that even the unlearned are considered exceedingly good. The condition for this goodness is karrar mun collatu irukka perin, meaning if they manage to stay without speaking in the presence of the learned. By remaining silent, they hide their ignorance and show respect, which earns them the reputation of being good people.

ai.literal: Unlearned man's cleverness, exceedingly good even if it is, will not accept, knowledge possessors.
ai.translation: Even if the natural cleverness of an unlearned man is exceedingly good, the wise will not accept it.
ai.modern: படிக்காதவனின் அறிவுக்கூர்மை மிகவும் நன்றாக இருந்தாலும், அறிவுடையவர்கள் அதனை ஏற்றுக்கொள்ள மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that natural cleverness without formal learning is not valued by the wise. The word 'கல்லாதான்' refers to a person who has not acquired learning, while 'ஒட்பம்' denotes natural brilliance or cleverness. Even if such a person's ideas seem exceptionally good ('கழிய நன்று'), those who possess true knowledge ('அறிவுடையார்') will not accept them, because uncultivated intellect lacks depth, discipline, and reliability.

ai.literal: Unlearned a person's dignity, having joined to speak, failure will suffer.
ai.translation: The apparent dignity of an unlearned person will shatter the moment he joins a gathering and begins to speak.
ai.modern: படிக்காத ஒருவனுடைய பெருமையானது, மற்றவர்களோடு சேர்ந்து பேசத் தொடங்கும் போது அழிந்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates how ignorance cannot be hidden by mere appearance. The word 'தகைமை' refers to the dignity or apparent worth a person might project. 'தலைப்பெய்து சொல்லாட' means joining a gathering of people to converse. As long as the unlearned person remains silent, their lack of knowledge is concealed. However, the moment they speak, their 'சோர்வு' (failure or slipping) occurs, exposing their true ignorance.

ai.literal: "They exist" that is said measure-they-are except, yielding-not barren land like-they-are learn-not-they.
ai.translation: The unlearned are exactly like barren land that yields nothing, except for the mere fact that they can be said to exist.
ai.modern: கல்லாதவர்கள் 'உயிரோடு இருக்கிறார்கள்' என்று சொல்லப்படும் அளவினரே தவிர, வேறு எந்தப் பயனும் தராத களர் நிலத்தைப் போன்றவர்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares uneducated people to barren, saline soil (களர்). Just as barren land occupies space but produces no crops, the unlearned occupy space in the world but produce nothing of value to themselves or others. The phrase 'உளர் என்னும் மாத்திரையர்' emphasizes that their only defining trait is their mere physical existence, while 'பயவா' (non-yielding) directly links the uselessness of the uncultivated land to the uncultivated mind.

ai.literal: Subtle excellent penetrating intellect he who lacks, beauty charm clay excellent fashioned doll like that.
ai.translation: The physical beauty of a person who lacks a subtle, excellent, and penetrating intellect is like that of a beautifully fashioned clay doll.
ai.modern: நுட்பமான, மாண்புடைய, ஆழமாக நுழையும் அறிவு இல்லாதவனுடைய உடல் அழகு, களிமண்ணால் சிறப்பாகச் செய்யப்பட்ட பொம்மையின் அழகைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares an uneducated person's physical attractiveness to a clay doll. The words 'nuṇ' (subtle), 'māṇ' (excellent), and 'nuḻai' (penetrating) describe the qualities of a refined intellect gained through learning. The word 'pulam' here takes the sense of intellect or knowledge rather than a field or sense organ. Without such an intellect, a person's outward beauty ('eḻil nalam') is lifeless and superficial, just like a doll made of earth ('maṇ') that looks beautiful but has no life or awareness inside.

ai.literal: With the good happened than poverty is indeed more painful, with the unlearned happened wealth.
ai.translation: Wealth possessed by the unlearned is far more grievous than poverty suffered by the good.
ai.modern: நல்லவர்களிடம் உள்ள வறுமையை விட, படிக்காதவர்களிடம் உள்ள செல்வம் மிகவும் துன்பம் தருவதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts two situations: poverty among the good and wealth among the unlearned. The comparative suffix 'இன்' (in) attached to 'வறுமை' (poverty) sets up the comparison, meaning 'than poverty'. The word 'இன்னாதே' (is indeed painful/grievous) emphasizes that it is worse for an uneducated person to have wealth than for a good, educated person to suffer poverty, as the unlearned are likely to misuse their wealth and cause harm.

ai.literal: High they-were-born even-if, unlearned-people, low having-been-born learned-people's that-measure they-are-without greatness.
ai.translation: Even if born in a high station, the unlearned do not possess the greatness of the learned who are born in a low station.
ai.modern: உயர்ந்த குடியில் பிறந்திருந்தாலும், கல்வி கற்காதவர்கள் தாழ்ந்த குடியில் பிறந்திருந்தாலும் கல்வி கற்றவர்களின் பெருமைக்கு ஈடாக மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts the value of birth with the value of education. It states that unlearned people, despite being born into a high social standing, lack true worth. In contrast, those who have learned possess a greatness that surpasses social origins, making them superior even if born into a lower station. The word 'பாடு' (pāṭu) here means greatness or dignity, emphasizing that true social worth comes from learning, not lineage.

ai.literal: With beasts, humans, they are like; shining books with the learned, the other people.
ai.translation: The unlearned are to those who have mastered illustrious books as beasts are to human beings.
ai.modern: விளங்குகின்ற சிறந்த நூல்களைக் கற்றவர்களோடு கல்லாதவர்களை ஒப்பிடுவது, மக்களோடு விலங்குகளை ஒப்பிடுவதற்குச் சமமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes a stark analogy: the unlearned are to the learned what beasts are to humans. The phrase 'இலங்கு நூல்' (shining books) emphasizes that true learning enlightens the mind. The poet uses the sociative case suffixes 'ஒடு' and 'ஓடு' (with / compared to) to set up the direct comparison between the two pairs. Just as humans possess higher faculties that distinguish them from animals, those who have studied possess a refined understanding that fundamentally elevates them above the ignorant.
